title: Tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost

concept.text: The innovation would be a cementitious composite that can carry substantial tension, continue deforming after cracks form, and support ordinary buildings without discrete steel reinforcement at a cost close to conventional reinforced concrete. Its scope includes beams, columns, walls, joints and potentially shells. The target is a complete structural material system, beyond a ductile laboratory specimen or repair product.

Engineered cementitious composites, or ECCs, provide a laboratory basis for this idea. Reinforcing fibers bridge cracks in the cementitious matrix, allowing tensile strain-hardening: after initial cracking, the composite can carry increasing tensile stress while developing further deformation and distributed cracking. The reported ductility belongs to the fiber–matrix composite; it is not an intrinsic tensile property of the mineral matrix alone. A structure without steel bars would therefore still contain reinforcement in the form of distributed fibers.

The defining advance would combine this tensile behavior with reliable structural-scale load paths, connections, construction methods and competitive installed cost. The supplied evidence establishes promising material behavior but does not demonstrate that combined capability in a steel-free building system.

significance.text: If achieved, the innovation would offer a major alternative to structures that rely on discrete steel bars to carry tension. Tensile resistance and crack control would instead be distributed through a fiber-reinforced cementitious composite. The laboratory evidence supports the underlying fiber-bridging mechanism; extending it to ordinary structural systems at competitive cost is the conditional revolutionary step.

As a prospective consequence, removing steel bars could simplify reinforcement placement and reduce dependence on bar congestion, reinforcement cover and protection against steel corrosion. It could also expand the design possibilities for thin members and shells. These are system-level possibilities, not demonstrated benefits of the supplied laboratory mixtures. Other durability mechanisms, fiber requirements, member dimensions and connection details could retain or introduce constraints.

Becoming a default construction material would require more than several-percent tensile strain. Fire resistance, long-term durability, construction reliability, connection performance, code acceptance and delivered cost would determine whether the material could compete broadly. Nor would replacing steel automatically make the structure low-carbon: binder production, fiber production, material quantities and service life would still matter. The supplied study's mechanical, economic and environmental comparisons illustrate why these objectives must be assessed together rather than inferred from ductility alone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is an economical combination of tensile ductility and complete steel-free structural performance. A small direct-tension specimen does not establish the behavior of beams, columns or joints under interacting gravity, lateral, shear and repeated loads. The proposed engineering challenge includes maintaining distributed cracking and deformation capacity while establishing dependable load transfer throughout a structure, especially at connections.

Material economy remains a concrete obstacle. The reviewed study identifies expensive polyvinyl alcohol, or PVA, fibers as a barrier to large-scale ECC application and documents the high binder content of conventional ECC. It does not isolate binder content's contribution to first cost. Cheaper fibers cannot simply be substituted while assuming the same performance: fully polypropylene-reinforced specimens in the study showed brittle tensile behavior. The breakthrough must preserve the required fiber–matrix interaction while reducing cost.

A proposed route to economy is a mixture compatible with coarse aggregate, or another approach that achieves comparable savings without sacrificing tensile performance. That route is not established by the supplied evidence. Additional barriers include reproducible mixing and fiber dispersion at construction scale, dependable behavior across member geometries, and adequate fire and durability performance. These should be treated as capabilities to establish, rather than administrative adoption tasks assumed to follow automatically from a successful material test.

current_state.text: Jiang and coauthors' study, published in Materials on 21 January 2026, reports laboratory results for limestone calcined clay cement composites, or LC3-ECC. With 2% polyethylene fiber, mixture L-W25S45-E reached an ultimate tensile strain of 8.40 ± 0.42%; the accompanying discussion identifies a superplasticizer dosage of 0.45% and notes a slight strength reduction. These are small-specimen direct-tension results, not measurements from a full-scale structural frame. The 7.78% value in the paper's Highlights concerns a different mixture and does not negate the Table 5 result.

The same study reports potentially substantial fiber-related mixture-cost reductions, but its numerical descriptions require reconciliation. The abstract and conclusions state that LC3-PP costs approximately half as much as LC3-PVA. Section 3.5 instead describes full polypropylene replacement as reducing cost to approximately one-quarter of conventional ECC cost, alongside a roughly 43% reduction discussed with ambiguous substitution wording. These statements cannot be treated as one settled ratio. They concern modeled ECC mixture costs, not installed structural-system costs relative to ordinary concrete, and the fully polypropylene-reinforced specimens lost the tensile ductility central to this concept.

The earlier research attributes to Lei and coauthors' review, listed as published on 15 April 2025, an M45-ECC cost of 4.1 times ordinary concrete, with CO2 and energy factors of 1.6 and 2.8. It also records a reference mixture containing 583 kg/m³ ordinary Portland cement, 700 kg/m³ fly ash, silica sand and 2% PVA fiber by volume. These figures remain unverified in the supplied evidence: the source index contains no retained article text, and the earlier research says a full-text PDF was not opened. They are preserved as attributed research claims, not confirmed quantitative benchmarks; their absence from the retained evidence does not establish that they are false.

The supplied review identifies the Jiang article and reports complete, untruncated text extraction, supporting interpretation of its prose and extracted tables. Figure images were not inspected, including Figure 16, so plotted cost values cannot resolve the economic discrepancy here. The earlier research also mentions specialty applications such as link slabs and coupling beams, but the supplied evidence does not establish their deployment scope or whether steel reinforcement was retained. No bounded freshness search was supplied, so the dated laboratory findings cannot establish the entire field's status as of 1 November 2026, including whether newer system demonstrations exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed structural demonstration: construct and test a multi-storey frame, or an integrated set of full-scale beams, columns, walls where relevant, and joints, without steel reinforcement. Demonstrate gravity and lateral resistance appropriate to a specified ordinary building design, distributed cracking, and deformation capacity comparable to a functionally equivalent ductile reinforced-concrete system. Component tests must establish the relevant system load paths and connection behavior; a frame test must include its consequential connections. A repair mortar, tensile coupon or isolated link slab would not meet this scope.
completion_criteria.label: Steel-free full-scale structural systems demonstrate building resistance and comparable ductility

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic demonstration: document total installed structural-system cost no greater than about twice that of the equivalent reinforced-concrete alternative. Use consistent accounting for both options, including material quantities, fibers, labor, formwork, connections and construction processes, with a bill of quantities and dated local prices. This twofold ceiling is an author-proposed milestone, not an established industry standard or a demonstration of price parity. Reaching ordinary cost more strictly would require a closer comparison with the conventional alternative.
completion_criteria.label: Installed structural-system cost stays within about twice reinforced-concrete cost

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility demonstration: repeat the material and structural results across independent batches and teams, disclose mixture proportions and processing requirements, and report variability, failure modes and sensitivity to construction conditions. Test a justified range of member sizes and loading histories. Such finite tests would establish the demonstrated breadth of the system, not literal suitability for every structure or exposure.
completion_criteria.label: Material and structural results reproduced across independent batches and teams

completion_criteria.text: General-use qualification would additionally require evidence for fire performance, long-term durability, sustained loading, construction quality control and applicable code acceptance. The demonstrated envelope should state its limits, including geometry, loading, environmental exposure and connection types. Passing a structural test and a cost milestone would be a convincing advance, but would not by itself complete these further qualifications.
completion_criteria.label: General-use qualification evidence and demonstrated application limits are reported

related_concepts.text: CIV-11, Default-cost reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior and no corrosion in ordinary exposures, is the closest alternative route in the supplied roster. It retains discrete reinforcement while seeking corrosion resistance at carbon-steel-like cost and behavior. CIV-05 instead seeks structural performance without steel reinforcement through a tensile-ductile composite. Their durability and economic objectives overlap, but a noncorroding bar does not make the surrounding mineral matrix ductile, and a ductile composite does not supply a replacement bar for existing reinforced-concrete practice. This comparison follows the supplied concept descriptions; no independent CIV-11 evidence was provided.

CIV-01, A primary structural binder at global cement scale without process carbon dioxide, concerns binder emissions and production scale. CIV-05 concerns tensile behavior and structural substitution. A low-emission binder could contribute to CIV-05, but neither capability establishes the other. CIV-10, Structural concrete that stores building-relevant energy, likewise adds a different material function; energy storage would not demonstrate tensile ductility, steel-free structural performance or competitive installed cost.

CIV-04, Repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking, concerns restoration after damage. CIV-05 seeks continued tensile resistance and distributed cracking during deformation; crack tolerance does not establish repeated healing or recovery. CIV-09, Immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake, at life-safety cost, shares an interest in deformation and damage control, but occupancy also depends on the wider building system. Demonstrating a ductile mineral frame would not by itself demonstrate immediate occupancy.

CIV-07, Load-bearing engineered living materials for ordinary structures, shares the ambition of an alternative structural material but requires a living-material capability that CIV-05 does not. CIV-12, Fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost, concerns adaptive structural behavior; the passive fiber-bridging mechanism discussed here does not establish adaptation or its fail-safe operation. These are roster-based distinctions, not assessments of either concept's demonstrated maturity.

unresolved_issues: The Lei review's reported cost, CO2 and energy ratios, reference-mixture quantities, comparison basis and wording remain unverified because no article text was retained.

The Jiang study's approximately-half, approximately-one-quarter and roughly-43% cost descriptions require reconciliation of mixtures, denominators and substitution wording. Figure 16 was not inspected.
The supplied evidence does not establish the extent or reinforcement details of link-slab and coupling-beam deployment, or the existence of a qualifying steel-free building demonstration.
No bounded freshness search establishes the field's status as of 1 November 2026.
The relative contributions of binder content, fiber choice and construction processes to competitive installed cost remain unresolved.
The proposed twofold installed-cost milestone requires justification for a specific market and building comparator; it is not ordinary-cost parity or an established standard.

The review recommended removing the unverified Lei numerical attribution from the corrected current-state claim. This record instead retains it explicitly as an unverified research attribution to preserve the supplied quantitative detail without asserting verification.

brief.title: Affordable buildings without steel reinforcing bars
possible: People could build ordinary buildings from a cement-based material that keeps carrying loads as it cracks and stretches, at a cost close to reinforced concrete. Fibers spread through the material would carry tension—the forces that pull it apart—without separate steel reinforcing bars.
why: Builders could spend less effort placing steel bars and protecting them against corrosion. Designers could gain more freedom to make thin building parts and curved shells, because fibers throughout the material would help carry pulling forces and control cracks.

sources.showed: This review surveys developments in cement-based composites reinforced with fibers, with a focus on reducing carbon emissions.
sources.cited_for: The review provides background on the material costs and environmental impacts of these composites.
sources.not_established: A review does not demonstrate an affordable building system without steel reinforcement.

sources.showed: Laboratory cement-based samples with plastic fibers continued stretching under tension after cracking. Using only cheaper polypropylene fibers, another plastic, produced brittle behavior.
sources.quote: In contrast, an increase in polypropylene fiber led to a degradation in crack-resistant properties.
sources.cited_for: The experiments support the material's ability to stretch after cracking and expose a tradeoff between fiber cost and performance.
sources.not_established: Small samples do not establish reliable building connections, full-size structural performance or competitive installed cost.

shown: Zhilu Jiang and colleagues reported that small cement-based samples reinforced with polyethylene, a plastic fiber, stretched by 8.40% before reaching their limit. This demonstrates material behavior in laboratory tension tests; it does not demonstrate a complete building system.
missing: Full-size building parts and their connections still need to carry combined loads reliably without steel reinforcement.
An economical mixture still needs to preserve stretching after cracking while remaining practical to mix and place on site.
Independent teams still need to reproduce the material and structural results under varied construction conditions.
Fire resistance, long-term durability and sustained-load performance still need to support general building use.

milestones.label: Full-size structures carry building loads without steel
milestones.explanation: A full-size frame or integrated set of building parts and joints would have to resist building loads and deform comparably to reinforced concrete without steel. This would establish dependable load transfer through the structure.

milestones.label: Installed cost stays within about twice reinforced concrete
milestones.explanation: Total installed cost would have to stay within about twice that of an equivalent reinforced-concrete structure, counting materials and construction consistently. This would establish an economic step toward ordinary cost.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce material and structural performance
milestones.explanation: Independent teams and batches would have to reproduce performance across justified member sizes and loading conditions, reporting processing needs, variability and failures. This would establish how broadly the results hold.

milestones.label: General building use has evidence and clear limits
milestones.explanation: Evidence would have to cover fire, durability, sustained loads, construction quality and code acceptance, with explicit application limits. This would establish where the system qualifies for general use.

uncertain: The study's cost comparisons need reconciliation, and mixture savings may not translate into lower installed building costs.
The proposed cost ceiling is not price parity, and its suitability depends on the market and building used for comparison.
Replacing steel does not automatically lower carbon emissions; cement ingredients, fibers, material quantities and service life all matter.

page.title: Strain-hardening cementitious composite buildings without rebar
page.definition: Buildings whose load-bearing superstructure uses strain-hardening cementitious composites (SHCC): cement-based materials with short fibers that carry increasing tensile stress after cracking, without reinforcing bars, mesh or prestressing tendons. Their installed structural cost is no greater than an equivalent reinforced-concrete design.

goal.need: A 2020 TxDOT assessment describes engineered cementitious composites (ECC) with 3–5% tensile strain capacity using 1.5–2% fibers by volume, but identifies initial cost as a barrier to large-volume applications. Eliminating reinforcing bars requires extending that tensile response through building members and connections. The polyethylene/polypropylene comparison shows that changing fibers can remove the tensile behavior sought.

figures.caption: Laboratory limestone–calcined-clay cement composites, published on 21 January 2026.
figures.note: Mixtures L-W25S45-E and L-W25S45-P contain 2% fiber by volume, with water/binder ratio 0.25 and superplasticizer dosage 0.45%. Specimens were tested after 28 days using an 80 mm gauge and 0.15 mm/min displacement rate. Direct-tension replicate counts are unspecified; ± values are reproduced as reported.

completion.title: A completed building without rebar obtains occupancy approval at reinforced-concrete installed cost or less.
completion.criterion: A completed building obtains final occupancy approval with an SHCC load-bearing superstructure, including connections and gravity and lateral load paths, without reinforcing bars, mesh or prestressing tendons. Its documented total installed superstructure cost is no greater than a code-compliant reinforced-concrete design for the same site, floor area, occupancy, loads, fire rating and design life. Both are priced for the same locality and month, including fibers, other materials, labor, formwork, equipment and connections.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no external combined building-performance and installed-cost threshold was located.
completion.basis: Searched JSCE HPFRCC recommendations, ICC alternative-material and occupancy provisions, the TxDOT ECC assessment and Michigan-led 3D-printing research for a combined structural-performance and installed-cost endpoint. No external cost-parity threshold for a complete building without rebar was located. The fallback joins official approval for one completed building to literal installed-cost parity.

milestones.title: A cementitious composite exceeds 0.5% mean tensile strain with mean crack width below 0.2 mm.
milestones.criterion: A short-fiber cementitious composite exhibits tensile strain hardening and multiple fine cracks, with average ultimate tensile strain >0.5% and average crack width <0.2 mm. Use JSCE Testing Methods 1–3, including at least five specimens for each tensile and crack-width test and approximately 0.5 mm/min deformation rate. Crack-width specimens are normally four weeks old. Jiang's results support material development but do not document qualification under these methods.
milestones.set_by: Japan Society of Civil Engineers, 2008 HPFRCC recommendations, Section 1.1(2) and Testing Methods 1–3; this is a material criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: average ultimate tensile strain determined with testing method 2 is more than 0.5 %

milestones.title: An SHCC building without bars receives building-code approval as an alternative structural system.
milestones.criterion: In a jurisdiction adopting the 2024 International Building Code, the building official approves the proposed SHCC structure without bars under Section 104.2.3. The system must satisfy code intent and equivalence in quality, strength, effectiveness, durability, safety and fire safety. Equivalence tests must have sufficient scale to predict end-use performance and be performed by a party acceptable to the official. Approval must cover the proposed members, connections and load paths.
milestones.set_by: International Code Council, 2024 IBC Section 104.2.3; existing provisions reproduced in the 2025 IADMIN agenda. Approval is issued by the building official where the code is adopted.
milestones.threshold_quote: be not less than the equivalent of that prescribed in this code

milestones.title: A completed SHCC building without bars receives a final certificate of occupancy.
milestones.criterion: The completed building receives a certificate of occupancy under 2024 IBC Section 111.2 after inspection finds no violations of the code or other laws enforced by the department; a temporary certificate does not qualify. Published construction evidence includes one 75 mm unreinforced ultra-high-ductility concrete shell for the 2021 China Flower Expo, described by Zhang and Huang in a paper published online on 25 October 2023.
milestones.set_by: International Code Council, 2024 IBC Sections 111.2–111.3; existing provisions reproduced in the 2025 IADMIN agenda. The certificate is issued by the local building official.
milestones.threshold_quote: the building official shall issue a certificate of occupancy
